title: 02. Data Structures: List as Stack, Queue, Deque
summary: Lists can implement classic data structures. Understanding WHEN to use which is key:

sections.title: CONCEPT
sections.body:
Lists can implement classic data structures. Understanding WHEN to use which is key:

```
STACK (LIFO):    append() + pop()           — O(1) both ends at back
QUEUE (FIFO):    append() + pop(0)          — O(1) append, O(n) pop!
DEQUE (Both):    collections.deque          — O(1) ALL operations
```

sections.title: 3 KEY EXAMPLES

quiz.question: Why is list.pop(0) O(n)?
options: This is one of Python's most subtle behaviors and causes real bugs: > > > > This trips people up in closures, function arguments, and class attributes: > > > My…
A shallow copy creates a new container object but fills it with references to the same objects as the original.
Both create empty lists, but there are subtle differences: > > > > Performance: [] is ~2x faster than list() because [] compiles to a single BUILD_LIST bytecode…
Because lists store elements in contiguous memory as an array.
quiz.explanation: Because lists store elements in contiguous memory as an array. When you remove the first element, all remaining elements must shift one position to the left to fill the gap. For n elements, that's n-1 shifts → O(n). pop() (last element) is O(1) — no shifting needed, just decrement the length counter.

quiz.question: What is the difference between deque.appendleft() and list.insert(0, x)?
options: itertools provides memory-efficient generators for common sequence operations: > > > > I use itertools extensively in data pipelines.
Behaviorally identical — both count occurrences of a value, scan the entire sequence O(n), return 0 if not found (no error).
Timsort is brilliantly optimized for real-world data that often has existing order.
Both insert at the front, but drastically different performance: > > - list.insert(0, x): O(n) — must shift ALL elements right to make room > - deque.appendleft(x): O(1)…
quiz.explanation: Both insert at the front, but drastically different performance: list.insert(0, x): O(n) — must shift ALL elements right to make room deque.appendleft(x): O(1) — doubly-linked structure, just update head pointer In practice: for any algorithm requiring frequent front-insertion or front-deletion (BFS, sliding window, LRU cache), always use deque.

quiz.explanation: Honestly, almost never for a pure queue. But there are valid scenarios: Very small queues (< 100 elements): the O(n) pop(0) is negligible, list is simpler to use When you need indexing: deque[i] is O(n) for middle elements; list[i] is O(1).
